problem: Jane's hedge "denoting, I thought, choler" is stated as fact; "I thought" is dropped.
final_text: Two wax candles stood lit on the table and two on the mantelpiece. Basking in the light and heat of a magnificent fire lay Pilot, with Adèle kneeling beside him. Half reclined on a couch was Mr. Rochester, his foot propped on a cushion. He was watching Adèle and the dog, the firelight full on his face. I recognized my traveller with his broad, dark eyebrows, his square forehead made squarer by the straight sweep of his black hair. I recognized his decisive nose, more notable for character than beauty, his full nostrils suggesting, I thought, a quick temper, his stern mouth, chin, and jaw—yes, all three were very stern, no mistake about it. His build, now free of its cloak, matched the squareness of his features. I suppose it was a good figure in the athletic sense—broad-chested and lean-flanked, though neither tall nor graceful.

problem: Source hedge "Adèle might perhaps spill it" becomes a definite "Adèle might spill it"; "perhaps" dropped.
final_text: "Will you hand Mr. Rochester his cup?" Mrs. Fairfax said to me. "Adèle might perhaps spill it."

problem: "over-modesty" (excessive modesty) is rendered "false modesty", which implies insincerity Rochester does not charge her with.
final_text: "Oh, don't retreat into excessive modesty! I have examined Adèle and find you have taken great pains with her. She is not bright, she has no talents; yet in a short time she has made real improvement."

problem: The folk phrase "the men in green" (the fairies), which Jane echoes back in the next paragraph, is replaced outright, and "that damned ice" is softened to "cursed", flattening Rochester's oath.
final_text: "For the men in green—the fairies. It was a perfect moonlit evening for them. Did I break through one of your rings, and you spread that damned ice on the road?"

problem: Jane's echo of Rochester's "The men in green" is lost (paired with 13.45).
final_text: I shook my head. "The men in green all left England a hundred years ago," I said, speaking as seriously as he had. "And not even in Hay Lane, or the fields around it, could you find a trace of them. I don't think summer, harvest, or winter moon will ever shine on their revels again."

problem: Rochester's Shakespearean allusion "the head and front of his offending" (Othello) is replaced by a plain paraphrase; the allusion should stay recognizable.
final_text: "And was that the head and front of his offending—the worst of it?" demanded Mr. Rochester.

problem: Source "Approach the table" means bring the table near, which Jane then does ("I wheeled it to his couch"); "Bring it to the table" suggests bringing the portfolio and makes the following "it" confusing.
final_text: "Bring the table over," he said, and I wheeled it to his couch. Adèle and Mrs. Fairfax came closer to see the pictures.

problem: "Where did you get your copies?" assumes she copied from existing pictures (hence "Out of my head"); "subjects" loses that suspicion.
final_text: "Where did you get the pictures you copied?"

problem: The narrator's self-correction "so, too, was the foreground; or rather, the nearest billows, for there was no land" is compressed so that the "or rather, the nearest billows" is lost.
final_text: The pictures were watercolours. The first showed clouds, low and dark, rolling over a swollen sea. The whole distance was in shadow; so was the foreground—or rather, the nearest waves, for there was no land. One gleam of light fell on a half-submerged mast, on which perched a cormorant, dark and large, its wings flecked with foam. Its beak held a gold bracelet set with gems, which I had painted in the most brilliant tints my palette could yield, with as much glittering detail as my brush could manage. Below the bird and mast, a drowned body was visible through the green water—a fair arm the only limb clearly seen, from which the bracelet had been washed or torn.

problem: "the hair streamed shadowy, like a beamless cloud torn by storm or by electric travail" loses "shadowy" and "beamless" (lightless).
final_text: The second picture showed only the dim peak of a hill in the foreground, with grass and leaves slanting as if blown by a breeze. Beyond and above spread a vast sky, dark blue as at twilight. Rising into the sky was a woman's shape, visible to the bust, painted in tints as dusky and soft as I could blend. The shadowy forehead was crowned with a star; the features below were seen as through a veil of vapour; the eyes shone dark and wild; the hair streamed in shadow, like a lightless cloud torn by storm or lightning. On the neck lay a pale glow like moonlight; the same faint gleam touched the trail of thin clouds from which this vision of the Evening Star rose and bowed.

problem: "sparkles of a more lurid tinge" (a ghastlier, more glaring hue) becomes "darker" sparks, an invented quality; "close serried" (tightly ranked) lances is also dropped.
final_text: The third showed the peak of an iceberg piercing a polar winter sky. A close-ranked line of northern lights raised their dim lances along the horizon. In the foreground, dwarfing these into distance, rose a colossal head tilted toward the iceberg and resting against it. Two thin hands, clasped beneath the forehead and propping it up, drew a black veil over the lower features. Only a bloodless brow, white as bone, and an eye—hollow and fixed, blank except for the glassiness of despair—were visible. Above the temples, amid folds of black cloth as vague and shapeless as cloud, gleamed a ring of white flame studded with sparks of a more lurid, ghastly hue. This pale crescent was "the likeness of a kingly crown;" what it crowned was "the shape which shape had none."

problem: "the drawings are, for a school-girl, peculiar" (unusual, strange) is upgraded to "extraordinary", turning a guarded judgment into outright praise.
final_text: "Not completely: you've caught the shadow of your thought, but no more, probably. You lacked enough of the artist's skill and knowledge to give it full life. Yet the drawings are, for a schoolgirl, unusual. As for the ideas behind them—they are otherworldly. Those eyes in the Evening Star you must have seen in a dream. How did you make them look so clear yet not at all bright? The planet above dims their light. And what meaning lies in their solemn depth? And who taught you to paint wind? There's a fierce gale in that sky and on that hilltop. Where did you see Latmos? For that is Latmos. There—put the drawings away!"

problem: Source is definite: he relished the kiss scarcely more than Pilot would have, "nor so much"; modern adds a hedge ("and perhaps less").
final_text: Adèle went to kiss him before leaving the room. He endured the embrace but barely seemed to enjoy it more than Pilot would have—or even as much.

problem: Rochester's rude "tête-à-tête with a brat" is softened to "alone with a child", flattening his tone.
final_text: "Ah! Well, come forward; sit down here." He drew a chair near his own. "I am not fond of children's chatter," he continued. "As the old bachelor I am, I have no pleasant associations with their prattle. It would be intolerable to spend an entire evening alone with a brat. Don't pull that chair farther away, Miss Eyre; sit down exactly where I placed it—if you please, that is. Confound these courtesies! I keep forgetting them. Nor do I particularly enjoy the company of simple-minded elderly ladies. By the way, I must be mindful of mine; it won't do to neglect her. She is a Fairfax, or married to one, and blood is said to be thicker than water."

problem: Source: "a round rejoinder, which, if not blunt, is at least brusque"; modern calls it a "blunt answer" and introduces "rude", reversing Rochester's hedge.
final_text: "Ah! My word! There is something unusual about you," he said. "You have the air of a little nun—quaint, quiet, serious, and simple, sitting there with your hands folded and your eyes generally cast down to the carpet (except, that is, when they are aimed piercingly at my face, as just now). And when someone asks you a question or makes a remark you must reply to, you come out with a round, ready answer that is, if not blunt, at least brusque. What do you mean by it?"

problem: "even in a blind, imperfect sense, put faith in the confidence" becomes "blind, instinctive way"; "imperfect" (the partialness of the trust) is replaced by an invented quality.
final_text: With this announcement he rose from his chair and stood leaning his arm on the marble mantelpiece. In that posture his build was plainly visible as well as his face—the unusual breadth of his chest, almost out of proportion with the length of his limbs. I am sure most people would have called him an ugly man. Yet there was so much unconscious pride in his bearing, so much ease in his manner, such complete indifference to his own appearance, so haughty a faith in the power of other qualities—inherent or acquired—to make up for the lack of mere good looks, that in watching him, you inevitably shared his indifference and, even in some blind, imperfect way, trusted his confidence.

problem: Jane answers Rochester's claim to "superiority" with "your claim to superiority depends on..."; "authority" shifts the term of the argument.
final_text: "I don't think, sir, that you have a right to command me merely because you are older than I, or because you have seen more of the world. Your claim to superiority depends on the use you have made of your time and experience."

problem: "Promptly spoken" becomes "Bluntly spoken" (a different judgment), and "Leaving superiority out of the question" becomes "Setting authority aside" (see 14.47).
final_text: "Humph! Promptly spoken. But I won't accept that, seeing as it would never suit my case—I have made a poor, not to say bad, use of both advantages. Setting superiority aside, then, you must still agree to take my orders now and then without being stung or hurt by the commanding tone. Will you?"

problem: "nothing free-born would submit to" (the idea of the free-born Briton) becomes "no one with any self-respect"; Rochester's retort in 14.56 turns on "free-born".
final_text: "I am sure, sir, I would never mistake informality for rudeness. One I rather like; the other, nothing free-born would submit to, even for a salary."

problem: "Most things free-born will submit to anything for a salary" becomes "Most people with self-respect will endure anything for a salary", a self-contradictory statement that distorts Rochester's cynical retort.
final_text: "Nonsense! Most things free-born will submit to anything for a salary. So keep your opinions to yourself and don't venture into generalizations you are wholly ignorant about. However, I mentally shake your hand for that answer, inaccurate as it is—as much for the way it was said as for its substance. The manner was frank and sincere; one does not often encounter such a manner. No, on the contrary, affectation, or coldness, or stupid, thick-headed misunderstanding of one's meaning are the usual rewards of candour. Not three in three thousand inexperienced school-girl governesses would have answered me as you just did. But I don't mean to flatter you. If you are made from a different mould than the majority, it is no credit to you—Nature did it. And after all, I go too fast in my conclusions. For all I know yet, you may be no better than the rest; you may have intolerable flaws to offset your few good points."

problem: Invented clause "when I have so much to answer for myself"; "I started, or rather ... was thrust on to a wrong tack" loses the active/passive self-correction (modern says "I was set on" then "pushed"); "lay half the blame" loses "half"; "a colour of life" becomes "a pattern of living".
final_text: "Yes, yes, you are right," he said. "I have plenty of faults of my own—I know it, and I don't wish to minimize them. God knows I have no business being too severe about others. I have a past—a series of actions, a colour of life—to contemplate in my own breast, which might well redirect my sneers and judgments from my neighbours to myself. I started—or rather (for like other wrongdoers, I like to lay half the blame on bad luck and hostile circumstances) I was pushed—onto a wrong course at the age of twenty-one, and I have never found my way back since. But I might have been very different. I might have been as good as you—wiser—nearly as untainted. I envy you your peace of mind, your clean conscience, your unspoiled memory. Little girl, a memory without stain or corruption must be an exquisite treasure—an inexhaustible source of pure refreshment. Isn't it?"

problem: "elected the involuntary confidant" becomes "unwilling keeper" (involuntary is not unwilling), and the Miltonic "such bad eminence" allusion disappears into "deep wickedness".
final_text: "Perfectly clear then—clean and healthy. No flood of foul water had turned it into a poisoned pool. I was your equal at eighteen—quite your equal. Nature meant me to be, on the whole, a good man, Miss Eyre—one of the better kind. And you see I am not. You would say you don't see it; at least I flatter myself I read that much in your eye (beware, by the way, what you express with that eye of yours; I am quick at reading its language). Then take my word for it—I am not a villain. You are not to think that, not to attribute to me any such bad eminence. But, owing I truly believe to circumstances rather than my natural inclination, I am an ordinary, commonplace sinner, worn out by all the petty vices that the rich and worthless use to pass the time. Does it surprise you that I confess this to you? Know that in the course of your future life you will often find yourself elected the involuntary keeper of other people's secrets. They will instinctively discover, as I have done, that it is not your way to talk about yourself, but to listen while others speak of themselves. They will feel, too, that you listen without malicious scorn at their indiscretion, but with a kind of natural sympathy—all the more comforting because it is so quietly given."

problem: "any vicious simpleton ... by his paltry ribaldry" becomes "some shallow fool ... cheap depravity": "vicious" is dropped and "ribaldry" (coarse talk) is escalated to "depravity".
final_text: "I know it well; and so I speak almost as freely as if I were writing my thoughts in a diary. You would say I should have been stronger than my circumstances; and I should have—I should have. But I was not. When fate wronged me, I lacked the wisdom to stay calm. I turned desperate; then I degenerated. Now, when some vicious fool disgusts me with his paltry vulgarity, I cannot flatter myself that I am better than he is. I am forced to admit that he and I are on the same level. I wish I had stood firm—God knows I do! Dread remorse when you are tempted to stray, Miss Eyre. Remorse is the poison of life."

problem: Source "I am paving hell with energy" is a riddle that puzzles Jane ("Sir?") and is explained only in 14.80 ("I am laying down good intentions"). Modern spells out "the road to hell with good intentions" here, so Jane's "Sir?" makes no sense and the joke's payoff is pre-empted.
final_text: "Well thought; well said, Miss Eyre. And at this very moment, I am paving hell with energy."

problem: "I am laying down good intentions" loses "good", which is the key to the proverb (hell is paved with good intentions); needed with the 14.78 fix.
final_text: "I am laying down good intentions, which I believe to be as solid as flint. My companions and pursuits shall certainly be different than they have been."

problem: Jane's quoted words "'Let it be right'" are paraphrased away, but in 14.92 Rochester answers "'Let it be right'—the very words. You have spoken them", which now refers to nothing.
final_text: "The power of saying of any strange, unsanctioned course of action, 'Let it be right.'"

problem: The anti-slavery catchphrase "a man and a brother" ("in the presence of a man and a brother—or father, or master, or what you will") is lost, and the modern adds "to call me".
final_text: "If you did, you would say it in such a grave, quiet way that I'd mistake it for wisdom. Do you never laugh, Miss Eyre? Don't bother answering—I can see you rarely laugh. But you can laugh very merrily: believe me, you are not naturally solemn any more than I am naturally wicked. The Lowood restraint still clings to you, controlling your features, muffling your voice, restricting your movements. In the presence of a man and a brother—or father, or master, or whatever you like—you are afraid to smile too freely, speak too openly, or move too easily. But in time, I think you will learn to be natural with me, as I find it impossible to be conventional with you. And then your looks and movements will have more life and variety than they dare to show now. I see, at intervals, the glance of a strange sort of bird through the close-set bars of a cage: a vivid, restless, resolute captive is in there; if it were free, it would soar to the clouds. You are still set on going?"

problem: "coquetry runs in her blood" (flirtatiousness, the link to Céline) becomes "Vanity", a different trait.
final_text: "Never mind—wait a moment. Adèle is not ready for bed yet. My position, Miss Eyre, with my back to the fire and my face to the room, gives me a good view. While talking to you, I have also been watching Adèle from time to time (I have my own reasons for finding her a curious study—reasons I may, indeed shall, share with you someday). She pulled from her box, about ten minutes ago, a little pink silk dress. Rapture lit her face as she unfolded it. Coquetry runs in her blood, blends with her mind, and seasons the marrow of her bones. 'Il faut que je l'essaie!' she cried, 'et à l'instant même!' and she rushed from the room. She is now with Sophie, being dressed up. In a few minutes she will come back, and I know what I shall see—a miniature of Céline Varens, as she used to appear on stage at the rise of—but never mind that. My tenderest feelings are about to receive a shock—such is my feeling. Stay now and see whether it comes true."

problem: Rochester's quoted French "'comme cela'" (echoing Adèle's line) is replaced by English "'just like that'"; the chapter otherwise keeps the French, so the echo should be kept.
final_text: "Pre-cise-ly!" was the answer. "And 'comme cela'—just like that—she charmed my English gold out of my British pockets. I have been green, too, Miss Eyre—oh, green as grass: no fresher shade colours you now than once coloured me. My Spring is gone, however, but it has left me this French flower on my hands, which, in some moods, I would gladly be rid of. Not valuing now the root it sprang from—having found it was a sort that nothing but gold dust could nourish—I have only half a fondness for the blossom, especially when it looks as artificial as it does just now. I keep it and raise it on the Roman Catholic principle of atoning for many sins, great or small, by one good deed. I'll explain all this someday. Goodnight."
